title: The Destroyer Destroyed and the King in His Beauty
summary: A final woe falls on the treacherous destroyer, while Jerusalem prays for the LORD's grace and he rises to scatter the nations. As the land mourns and treaties are broken, sinners in Zion ask who can live with the consuming fire, and the answer is the one who walks in righteousness. The chapter ends with a vision of Zion secure, a tent that will never be pulled up, where the people see the King in his beauty, the LORD is Judge, lawgiver, and King, and no one says, "I am sick."
story: Chapter 33 closes the series of woes that began in chapter 28. Five of those woes were aimed at Israel and Judah; this last one is aimed at the enemy, the destroyer who has not yet been destroyed. The chapter pulls together the section's themes: false trust gives way to prayer, judgment to cleansing, and the fear of Assyria to the sight of the true King. It also prepares for chapters 34 and 35, a final pair of chapters contrasting judgment on the nations with the joyful return of the redeemed, and for the narrative of chapters 36 and 37, where the destroyer actually arrives at Jerusalem's walls.
historical:
The destroyer is not named, but most interpreters identify him with Assyria, and specifically with Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC. Verse 8's broken treaty and despised witnesses fit the account in 2 Kings 18:14-17: Hezekiah admitted his rebellion, paid Sennacherib a heavy tribute of silver and gold, and yet the Assyrian king still sent his officials and an army against Jerusalem. The "envoys of peace" weeping in verse 7 may be Hezekiah's negotiators returning with nothing. Verse 18 recalls the officials of an occupying power who counted tribute and surveyed the city's defenses.

The places named in verse 9 were the most fertile and wooded regions of the land: Lebanon to the north with its forests, the Plain of Sharon along the coast, Bashan east of the Sea of Galilee with its oaks and pastures, and Mount Carmel near the coast. When these wither, the whole land is in mourning. Some interpreters take the chapter as a liturgy used in worship during or after the crisis, which would explain its mix of prayer, oracle, and hymn.
cultural:
Verses 14 to 16 follow the pattern of the entrance liturgies found in Psalms 15 and 24, where worshipers approaching the temple asked who could stand in God's presence and received an answer describing a righteous life. Here the question is asked in terror: who can dwell with a consuming fire? The answer lists concrete behaviors from ancient public life: refusing extortion, refusing bribes (which were a constant temptation for judges and officials), and refusing to listen to talk of murder.

Verse 20 pictures Jerusalem as a tent that will never be moved, drawing on Israel's memory of the tabernacle and of life in tents, when tent pegs could be pulled up at any time. Verses 21 and 23 add a surprising image for a city without a great river: Jerusalem will have the LORD himself as its broad rivers, but no enemy warship will sail on them. Great cities like Nineveh and Babylon depended on their rivers for defense and trade; Zion's security is God himself. The enemy's ship, with slack ropes and no sail, becomes plunder so abundant that even the lame can carry some off.
literary: The chapter is a mosaic of forms: a woe (verse 1), a communal prayer (verses 2 to 4), a hymn of confidence (verses 5 and 6), a lament over the land (verses 7 to 9), a divine oracle (verses 10 to 13), an entrance liturgy (verses 14 to 16), and a vision of the future (verses 17 to 24). Verse 1 is built on wordplay, repeating the roots for destroying and betraying so that the destroyer's own actions come back on him. Verse 10's threefold "Now" marks the turning point, as the LORD rises to act. The chapter ends where it began, with salvation, but it has moved from a people pleading "be gracious to us" to a people forgiven and healed.

outline.t: Prayer for grace and confidence in the exalted LORD
Broken treaties and a mourning land
The LORD rises: the nations consumed as chaff
Who can dwell with the consuming fire?
Zion secure: the King in his beauty and a forgiven people

doctrines.note: God is a consuming fire (verse 14), and his holiness is a threat to sinners in Zion as much as to foreign nations. Only a life of righteousness can dwell with him, which raises the question of how sinners can be made fit for his presence.
Verse 22 names the LORD as Judge, lawgiver, and King, uniting every function of government in God himself. His rule is the city's security and its salvation.
The chapter ends with a people forgiven of iniquity and freed from sickness (verse 24). Salvation is both forgiveness and the healing of the whole person and community.

words.note: Bagad, to act treacherously. Verse 1 uses it four times of the destroyer who betrays and will be betrayed. It describes the breaking of a trust or agreement, which fits Assyria's treatment of Hezekiah after he paid tribute.

Yophi, beauty. Used of human attractiveness and of splendid things, here it describes the King whom the people will see (verse 17). After the ugliness of siege and betrayal, the vision of the King's beauty is the heart of the promise.

Nasa, to lift or carry, and so to forgive. Forgiveness in Hebrew is often pictured as lifting and carrying away guilt. Verse 24 says the people will be forgiven their iniquity, literally that it will be lifted from them.

christ: The vision of seeing "the King in His beauty" (verse 17) is fulfilled, in Christian reading, in Jesus, the king who came to Zion. John says that the Word became flesh and "we have seen His glory" (John 1:14), and Revelation promises that God's servants will see his face (Revelation 22:4). The question of verse 14, who can dwell with the consuming fire, is answered in the New Testament by Christ, the only one who fully walked in righteousness, and who makes sinners righteous through his death so that they can come near. Hebrews 12:28-29 takes up the same language, calling God a consuming fire and urging worship with reverence and awe. The final promise, a forgiven people among whom no one is sick, is echoed in Jesus' healings and forgiveness together (Mark 2:1-12) and in the city of Revelation 21:4 where there is no more pain.
questions: Verse 6 calls the fear of the LORD Zion's treasure. What does it mean to treat reverence for God as a treasure rather than a burden?

The answer to who can dwell with God (verses 15 and 16) is very practical: no bribes, no extortion, no listening to violent plots. Why does the Bible tie nearness to God so closely to ordinary honesty?
What would it change for you to believe that you will one day see the King in his beauty?
